summary.text: The Cenozoic is Earth's current geological era, covering the last 66 million years of the planet's history.
It began with the Cretaceous–Paleogene extinction, and the loss of so many groups let mammals and birds diversify until large ones dominated life on Earth.
It is divided into the Paleogene, Neogene and Quaternary periods, and its relatively young, well-preserved rocks make it known in more detail than any other era.

facts.label: Name meaning
facts.value: 'New life', from Greek kainós and zōḗ

items.prompt: Why is the Cenozoic often called the Age of Mammals?

options.label: Mammals first appeared at its very start
Mammals were the dominant land animals in both hemispheres
Mammals were the only animals to survive into it
Mammals moved from the sea onto land during it

items.explain: The land animals that dominated both hemispheres in the Cenozoic were mammals: placentals in the north and marsupials in the south.

items.prompt: Paleozoic means 'old life' and Mesozoic means 'middle life'. What does Cenozoic mean?

options.label: New life
Late life
Cold life
Mammal life

items.explain: Cenozoic comes from Greek words for 'new' and 'life', fitting the pattern of the Mesozoic and Paleozoic names.

items.prompt: In the middle of the Eocene, a new ocean current formed between Australia and Antarctica. What followed?

options.label: Global warming that let jungles reach the poles
A rise in sea level that flooded the continents
Global cooling that shrank the jungles
A long drought that ended all grasslands

items.explain: The Antarctic Circumpolar Current disrupted ocean currents worldwide, causing a global cooling effect that shrank the jungles.

items.prompt: Why do geologists know more about the Cenozoic than about any other era?

options.label: It is the longest era in Earth's history
Its rocks are all found on a single continent
Humans recorded most of it in writing
Its rocks are relatively young and well preserved

items.explain: Knowledge of the Cenozoic is more detailed than of any other era because its rocks are relatively young and well preserved.

items.prompt: After the K–Pg extinction wiped out the large plant-eating animals, what happened to the land's vegetation in the Paleocene?

options.label: Open grasslands covered most continents
Dense but usually species-poor forests spread
Most land became bare desert for millions of years
Flowering plants vanished and ferns took over

items.explain: The extinction of large herbivores permitted the spread of dense but usually species-poor forests.

items.prompt: Grasslands expanded during the Oligocene, and many new species evolved. Which animals first appeared then?

options.label: Trilobites and sea scorpions
Dinosaurs and flying pterosaurs
Elephants, cats and dogs
The earliest fish with jaws

items.explain: The spread of grasslands in the Oligocene led many new species to evolve, including the first elephants, cats and dogs.
